chunk_findings.detail: `parse` validates stream-event names by doing `e in EVENTS` without first requiring `e` to be a string. With the usual closed-set representation of `EVENTS` as a hash set/frozenset, a hostile descriptor table such as `{"stream_events": [[]]}` makes the generator expression attempt to hash the list and raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` instead of the intended `EngineError("limit_detect.stream_events: names from ...")`. This is a bad-path crash in the engine’s validation layer.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/limit_detect.py:41

chunk_findings.detail: `render_json` uses Python’s default `json.loads`, which accepts non-JSON constants `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity`, and then uses default `json.dumps`, which re-emits those floats as `NaN`/`Infinity`. Because the function is supposed to preserve sibling entries and return JSON text, an existing file containing an unquoted `NaN` in an unrelated server entry is accepted and rewritten as invalid RFC 8259 JSON. For example, with any valid `launch` for `mcpconfig.SHAPE_MCP_SERVERS`, `render_json(..., existing='{"mcpServers": {"old": {"command": "x", "args": [NaN]}}}')` returns a document containing `NaN`, which strict JSON consumers used by agents will reject. The parser/serialiser should reject non-JSON constants or serialise with `allow_nan=False` and convert that to `EngineError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/mcp_shape.py:render_json

chunk_findings.detail: `run` uses `subprocess.run(..., capture_output=True)` and only then applies `limits.probe_output_bytes` to `(p.stdout + p.stderr)`. `subprocess.run` reads the child's entire stdout/stderr into memory before line 83, so the declared output cap does not bound the pipe reads. Given an allowed probe such as `[["/tmp/huge", "--version"]]`, where `/tmp/huge` is an executable whose basename is not in `SHELLS` and which prints bytes in a loop when passed `--version`, `parse` accepts the argv and `run` can exhaust memory/OOM before truncation; `p.stdout + p.stderr` also allocates a second full copy. This defeats the intended output cap and the hostile huge-output case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:83

chunk_findings.detail: The shell check extracts the basename with `rsplit("/", 1)` and compares it case-sensitively to `SHELLS`, so Windows shell paths can bypass it. For example, `render(["C:\\Windows\\System32\\cmd.exe", "/c", "{prompt_file}"], {"prompt_file": "x"})` passes `_lint` and returns an argv whose executable is `cmd.exe`, because the basename computed with `/` is the full backslash path, not `cmd.exe`. Likewise, `["C:/Windows/System32/WindowsPowerShell/v1.0/powershell.exe", "-Command", "{prompt_file}"]` passes because `powershell.exe` is not in `SHELLS`. This violates the stated invariant that the executable is never a shell.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/render_argv.py:70

chunk_findings.detail: `_lint` checks that the argv template is non-empty but does not check that `argv[0]` is a non-empty executable. Given `render(["", "x"], {})`, `_lint` accepts the template and `render` returns `Rendered(argv=("", "x"))`. An empty argv[0] cannot be launched (`execve`/`CreateProcess` will fail), so an invalid launch template is silently accepted instead of being rejected with `EngineError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/render_argv.py:53

chunk_findings.detail: The ReDoS audit treats only repeats with an upper bound greater than 1 as “ambiguous,” so a repeat of an optional subpattern is accepted. With the shipped `Limits` defaults, `safe_regex('(a?){256}b')` passes the audit: the outer repeat has `hi == limits.max_repeat == 256`, and the inner `a?` has `av[1] == 1`, so `_ambiguous` returns false. Calling `search(rx, 'a' * 128)` (no trailing `b`, and well under `max_match_chars=4096`) makes Python’s backtracking engine explore on the order of `C(256, 128)` ways to distribute 128 `a` characters among 256 optional groups before failing, which hangs. This is a concrete hostile pattern that bypasses the claimed ReDoS-safe-by-construction guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/safety.py:_ambiguous

chunk_findings.detail: `map_line` evaluates `not line.strip()` before the length guard. For a hostile line such as `line = " " + "x" * 10_000_000` with `limits.max_line_chars = 1024`, `line.strip()` is executed first and can allocate a nearly 10 MB copy before `len(line) > limits.max_line_chars` rejects the line. The line is supposed to be skipped immediately because it is too long, but this order does potentially expensive work and can exhaust memory or cause large allocation churn on many such lines.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/stream_map.py:84

chunk_findings.detail: `parse_rules` treats the mere presence of `exists` as satisfying the “exactly one test” rule, then stores `exists=bool(when.get("exists"))`. A rule like `{"when": {"path": "x", "exists": False}, "emit": "started"}` parses successfully, but `_matches` skips the exists branch and falls through to the equals branch with `equals=None`; that branch requires `v is not None`, so it never matches either `{"x": 1}` or `{}`. Thus `exists=false` is accepted as valid but silently creates a dead rule instead of being rejected or matching absence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/stream_map.py:66

chunk_findings.detail: `resolve_path` validates the template and the `home`/`dir` values separately but never validates the path after substitution, while `parse` only rejects literal `..` segments in the template. Given a descriptor like `{"path": "{home}../etc/passwd", "format": "jsonl", "fields": {"role": "role", "text": "text", "usage": "usage", "model": "model", "ts": "ts"}}`, `parse` accepts the path because its `/`-split segments are `["{home}..", "etc", "passwd"]` (no exact `..` segment). Calling `resolve_path(spec, home="/tmp/")` also passes validation because `"/tmp/"` is absolute and has no `..` segment, but the function returns `"/tmp/../etc/passwd"`, which resolves to `/etc/passwd` on POSIX. This lets the engine map/read a transcript outside the directory named by the template.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/transcript_map.py:resolve_path

chunk_findings.detail: The probe tests accept and execute an arbitrary executable path, including a shell script, as “safe argv.” The test creates `tmp_path/slow` containing `#!/bin/sh` and `sleep 5`, then expects `probe.parse([[str(slow), "--version"]])` to succeed and `probe.run` to execute it. This invokes `/bin/sh` despite the stated “no shell” constraint and despite `test_probe_refuses_what_is_not_declared_safe` expecting `["sh", "--version"]` to be refused. A descriptor that can name an arbitrary path can therefore bypass the shell ban by pointing to a shell script (or any executable), so the closed/declared-safe probe rule is not enforced by the behavior these tests assert.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_engines.py:test_probe_missing_binary_is_unavailable_and_timeouts_are_bounded

chunk_findings.detail: `render_json` now rejects `NaN`/`Infinity` literals on input, but the new output guard `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` is outside the `try` that converts JSON errors into `EngineError`. A syntactically valid JSON number that overflows to infinity, e.g. an existing file containing a sibling entry `"other": 1e999`, is loaded by `json.loads` as `float("inf")` because `parse_constant` is not invoked for numeric literals. Then `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` raises `ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant`, so a bad existing file crashes with an unhandled `ValueError` instead of returning text or raising `EngineError("the existing file is not JSON: ...")`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/mcp_shape.py:63

chunk_findings.detail: `_run_capped` does not stop processing the rest of a `select` result once the byte cap is crossed. With `limits.probe_output_bytes = 10`, if the child has 11 bytes ready on stdout and 65536 bytes ready on stderr, the first `os.read` appends 10 bytes and sets `total = 11`; the loop then reads stderr and evaluates `data[: limits.probe_output_bytes - total]`, i.e. `data[: -1]`, which appends 65535 bytes. The function returns roughly 65545 bytes and only then kills the child, so the declared output cap is bypassed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:_run_capped

chunk_findings.detail: The function computes `deadline` for the `select` loop but then calls `child.wait(timeout=limits.probe_timeout_s)` with a fresh full timeout after the pipes reach EOF. A probe that closes stdout/stderr at `probe_timeout_s - 0.05` and then sleeps for another `probe_timeout_s` causes the wait to run until nearly `2 * probe_timeout_s` before `stop_group` is called. The wait should use the remaining time from the original deadline, not a new full timeout.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:_run_capped

chunk_findings.detail: `_run_capped` uses `select.select` on pipe file descriptors. On Windows, `select.select` supports only sockets, so after `proc.spawn_stdio` succeeds the call raises `OSError` (e.g. WinError 10038) for any probe; because the exception occurs before the `stop_group` cleanup, the spawned child can also be left running. The parser explicitly treats backslash paths as Windows-style paths, so this is a defect in the intended cross-platform path handling.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:_run_capped

chunk_findings.detail: `is_shell` only removes a final `.exe` after lowercasing the last path component, so it does not handle Windows file-name forms whose trailing dot or space is stripped by the OS. Given the Windows launch template `["C:\\Windows\\System32\\cmd.exe.", "/c", "{prompt_file}"]` and values `{"prompt_file": "x"}`, `_lint` computes basename `cmd.exe.`, `removesuffix(".exe")` leaves it unchanged, and the value is not in `SHELLS`; the template is accepted. On Windows, the trailing dot is stripped during file-name resolution, so the accepted argv actually launches `cmd.exe`, violating the “no shell” invariant. A trailing space such as `cmd.exe ` has the same effect.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/render_argv.py:is_shell

chunk_findings.detail: `max_optional` is intended to bound the number of optional/alternation choices (`?` and `|`), but `_audit` adds `1` to `tally["narrow"]` for an entire `BRANCH` node rather than per alternative/pipe. With the shipped defaults, the pattern `a*(a|[a]|[aa])` repeated eight times followed by `a*b` (length 101, under `max_pattern_chars=200`) passes the audit: it has two wide repeats (`a*`), eight branch groups (`narrow=8`, not `>8`), and no repeat of a variable body. Calling `search(rx, "a" * 2048)` forces the regex engine to try the three alternatives in each of the eight groups across the two star splits before the trailing `b` fails, on the order of `3**8 * 2048**2` backtracks, so the new ReDoS limit is bypassed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/safety.py:_audit

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to guard the “length checked before `strip()`” fix, but its assertion cannot distinguish the two orderings. For the input `" " + "x" * 5000` with `Limits(max_line_chars=100)`, both the intended implementation (`len(line) > limit` before `line.strip()`) and the old implementation (`line.strip()` first, then the length check) return `None`; the only difference is that the old implementation allocates the large stripped copy. Because the test only asserts `is None`, it also passes with the old, unsafe ordering and therefore does not actually refute the earlier memory/allocation regression.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_engines.py:test_stream_map_checks_length_before_stripping

data.summary: After `ddflow gate run <id> ci` was cut by the harness timeout and ended, `gate status` showed ci as "[!] queued 11m of 15m elapsed" indefinitely with no result. A SIGTERMed `ddflow review` recorded both gates as terminated; a second background review then ran alongside a still-live first one (two `ddflow review DRV-engines` processes, no lock), duplicating reviewer cost. Repro: pgrep -fa "[d]dflow review" while two were started for one item.
data.title: gate status keeps a cut-off ci run as "queued 11m of 15m" forever; interrupted review leaves two concurrent review loops

data.body:
Fixes bug B8664a1e0c6: After `ddflow gate run <id> ci` was cut by the harness timeout and ended, `gate status` showed ci as "[!] queued 11m of 15m elapsed" indefinitely with no result. A SIGTERMed `ddflow review` recorded both gates as terminated; a second background review then ran alongside a still-live first one (two `ddflow review DRV-engines` processes, no lock), duplicating reviewer cost. Repro: pgrep -fa "[d]dflow review" while two were started for one item. Found on DRV-engines.

Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code; then `ddflow complete fix-B8664a1e0c6 --regression-test <test>` closes the bug with the task (or `ddflow bug fixed B8664a1e0c6 --regression-test <test>` first).

chunk_findings.detail: `render_json` wraps `json.loads` failures as `EngineError`, but the final `json.dumps(data, indent=2, allow_nan=False)` is not wrapped. Since `json.loads` uses Python's default `parse_float=float`, valid JSON numeric literals like `1e400` are accepted and become `float('inf')` without `_no_constant` being called. `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` then raises a raw built-in `ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant`. Given `render_json("mcpServers", "s", {"command":"c"}, existing='{"x": 1e400}')`, the function crashes with an unhandled `ValueError` instead of returning the rewritten config or an `EngineError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/mcp_shape.py:render_json

chunk_findings.detail: The path/script restriction is only a literal check on `argv[0]` for `/`, `\`, or `is_shell(argv[0])`; it never inspects the executable that `shutil.which(argv[0])` actually resolves to. With `allow_paths=False`, input like `[["myprobe", "--version"]]` passes `parse` when `myprobe` is an executable shell script found on PATH (or in the current directory if PATH contains `.`/empty). `run` then executes that script at line 128 via `[exe, *argv[1:]]`, so a shebang shell can run arbitrary code. This violates the stated “no shell / bad path” boundary.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:54

chunk_findings.detail: `run` marks every `_run_capped` result as `status="verified"`, except when `_run_capped` returns `None`. But `_run_capped` also returns a truncated output when `probe_output_bytes` is exceeded; if the child already exited normally, the exit code can be 0. For example with `probe_output_bytes=16`, a `tool --help` that prints 1KB and exits 0 produces `{"status": "verified", "exit_code": 0, "output": "<first 16 bytes>"}` with no `truncated` field or `unavailable` reason. A huge hostile output is reported as a complete verified fact.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:138

chunk_findings.detail: The output cap can be exceeded because the read truncation uses `total` before adding the chunk, but then adds the full `len(data)`. If the first selected fd overshoots the remaining cap, the next selected fd receives a negative slice stop. With `probe_output_bytes=100`, a child writing 200 bytes to stdout and 200 bytes to stderr before `select` returns both fds: stdout makes `total=200`, then stderr appends `data[:-100]` (the first 100 bytes), yielding 200 bytes of output despite the 100-byte cap.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:97-98

chunk_findings.detail: `is_shell("/bin/ash")` returns `False` because `SHELLS` omits common shells such as `ash` (the default shell on Alpine). Thus `_lint` accepts `["/bin/ash", "-c", "echo hi"]`; the rendered argv then runs a shell despite the module’s “never a shell” guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: `render_argv.py:is_shell`

chunk_findings.detail: For `env={1: "SECRET"}`, the iteration yields `child=1`, and `not _ENV_NAME.fullmatch(child)` calls `re.Pattern.fullmatch` with an `int`, raising `TypeError` instead of the intended `EngineError`. The validation should check `not isinstance(child, str)` before calling `fullmatch`, as it already does for `source`.
chunk_findings.title: `render_argv.py:render`

chunk_findings.detail: In `_children`, for `_c.BRANCH` the parsed operand is `(None, alt1, alt2, ...)`, but the function returns `list(av[1])` instead of `list(av[1:])`. This makes `_audit` traverse only the first alternative of a `|` branch, so any later alternative is never checked for nested quantifiers or back-references. Concretely, `safe_regex(r"b|(a+)+!")` passes the audit because only the harmless first alternative `b` is inspected, then `re.compile` accepts the catastrophic second alternative. On the default limits, `search(compiled, "a"*2048)` makes the engine backtrack over all 2048 `a`s, defeating the ReDoS protection this module is intended to provide.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/safety.py:57 (_children)

chunk_findings.detail: `parse_rules` accepts `when.equals = None` (`Rule.equals` is typed `str | int | float | bool | None`), but `_matches` returns `v is not None and type(v) is type(rule.equals) and v == rule.equals`. Since `_dig` returns `None` both for a JSON `null` and for a missing path, the first conjunct is `False` for a line like `{"x": null}`, so `map_line` returns `None` and no event is emitted. The `exists` predicate has the same problem at line 78: a present JSON `null` is treated as absent. Thus a valid accepted rule using `null` is silently dead.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/stream_map.py:78,81

chunk_findings.detail: The test aims to ensure `stream_map.map_line` checks the line length before stripping, but the input `" " + "x" * 5000` with `Limits(max_line_chars=100)` has a stripped length of 5000, which still exceeds the limit. Therefore an implementation that strips first and then applies the length check would also return `None`, so the test passes regardless of the ordering it claims to enforce. A distinguishing input would be one with pre-strip length > 100 and post-strip length ≤ 100, such as `" " * 5 + "x" * 96`; the current test cannot detect a strip-before-length-check regression.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_engines.py:test_stream_map_checks_length_before_stripping

chunk_findings.detail: `parse` validates stream-event names by doing `e in EVENTS` without first requiring `e` to be a string. With the usual closed-set representation of `EVENTS` as a hash set/frozenset, a hostile descriptor table such as `{"stream_events": [[]]}` makes the generator expression attempt to hash the list and raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` instead of the intended `EngineError("limit_detect.stream_events: names from ...")`. This is a bad-path crash in the engine’s validation layer.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/limit_detect.py:41

chunk_findings.detail: `render_json` uses Python’s default `json.loads`, which accepts non-JSON constants `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity`, and then uses default `json.dumps`, which re-emits those floats as `NaN`/`Infinity`. Because the function is supposed to preserve sibling entries and return JSON text, an existing file containing an unquoted `NaN` in an unrelated server entry is accepted and rewritten as invalid RFC 8259 JSON. For example, with any valid `launch` for `mcpconfig.SHAPE_MCP_SERVERS`, `render_json(..., existing='{"mcpServers": {"old": {"command": "x", "args": [NaN]}}}')` returns a document containing `NaN`, which strict JSON consumers used by agents will reject. The parser/serialiser should reject non-JSON constants or serialise with `allow_nan=False` and convert that to `EngineError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/mcp_shape.py:render_json

chunk_findings.detail: `run` uses `subprocess.run(..., capture_output=True)` and only then applies `limits.probe_output_bytes` to `(p.stdout + p.stderr)`. `subprocess.run` reads the child's entire stdout/stderr into memory before line 83, so the declared output cap does not bound the pipe reads. Given an allowed probe such as `[["/tmp/huge", "--version"]]`, where `/tmp/huge` is an executable whose basename is not in `SHELLS` and which prints bytes in a loop when passed `--version`, `parse` accepts the argv and `run` can exhaust memory/OOM before truncation; `p.stdout + p.stderr` also allocates a second full copy. This defeats the intended output cap and the hostile huge-output case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:83

chunk_findings.detail: The shell check extracts the basename with `rsplit("/", 1)` and compares it case-sensitively to `SHELLS`, so Windows shell paths can bypass it. For example, `render(["C:\\Windows\\System32\\cmd.exe", "/c", "{prompt_file}"], {"prompt_file": "x"})` passes `_lint` and returns an argv whose executable is `cmd.exe`, because the basename computed with `/` is the full backslash path, not `cmd.exe`. Likewise, `["C:/Windows/System32/WindowsPowerShell/v1.0/powershell.exe", "-Command", "{prompt_file}"]` passes because `powershell.exe` is not in `SHELLS`. This violates the stated invariant that the executable is never a shell.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/render_argv.py:70

chunk_findings.detail: `_lint` checks that the argv template is non-empty but does not check that `argv[0]` is a non-empty executable. Given `render(["", "x"], {})`, `_lint` accepts the template and `render` returns `Rendered(argv=("", "x"))`. An empty argv[0] cannot be launched (`execve`/`CreateProcess` will fail), so an invalid launch template is silently accepted instead of being rejected with `EngineError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/render_argv.py:53

chunk_findings.detail: The ReDoS audit treats only repeats with an upper bound greater than 1 as “ambiguous,” so a repeat of an optional subpattern is accepted. With the shipped `Limits` defaults, `safe_regex('(a?){256}b')` passes the audit: the outer repeat has `hi == limits.max_repeat == 256`, and the inner `a?` has `av[1] == 1`, so `_ambiguous` returns false. Calling `search(rx, 'a' * 128)` (no trailing `b`, and well under `max_match_chars=4096`) makes Python’s backtracking engine explore on the order of `C(256, 128)` ways to distribute 128 `a` characters among 256 optional groups before failing, which hangs. This is a concrete hostile pattern that bypasses the claimed ReDoS-safe-by-construction guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/safety.py:_ambiguous

chunk_findings.detail: `map_line` evaluates `not line.strip()` before the length guard. For a hostile line such as `line = " " + "x" * 10_000_000` with `limits.max_line_chars = 1024`, `line.strip()` is executed first and can allocate a nearly 10 MB copy before `len(line) > limits.max_line_chars` rejects the line. The line is supposed to be skipped immediately because it is too long, but this order does potentially expensive work and can exhaust memory or cause large allocation churn on many such lines.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/stream_map.py:84

chunk_findings.detail: `parse_rules` treats the mere presence of `exists` as satisfying the “exactly one test” rule, then stores `exists=bool(when.get("exists"))`. A rule like `{"when": {"path": "x", "exists": False}, "emit": "started"}` parses successfully, but `_matches` skips the exists branch and falls through to the equals branch with `equals=None`; that branch requires `v is not None`, so it never matches either `{"x": 1}` or `{}`. Thus `exists=false` is accepted as valid but silently creates a dead rule instead of being rejected or matching absence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/stream_map.py:66

chunk_findings.detail: `resolve_path` validates the template and the `home`/`dir` values separately but never validates the path after substitution, while `parse` only rejects literal `..` segments in the template. Given a descriptor like `{"path": "{home}../etc/passwd", "format": "jsonl", "fields": {"role": "role", "text": "text", "usage": "usage", "model": "model", "ts": "ts"}}`, `parse` accepts the path because its `/`-split segments are `["{home}..", "etc", "passwd"]` (no exact `..` segment). Calling `resolve_path(spec, home="/tmp/")` also passes validation because `"/tmp/"` is absolute and has no `..` segment, but the function returns `"/tmp/../etc/passwd"`, which resolves to `/etc/passwd` on POSIX. This lets the engine map/read a transcript outside the directory named by the template.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/transcript_map.py:resolve_path

chunk_findings.detail: The probe tests accept and execute an arbitrary executable path, including a shell script, as “safe argv.” The test creates `tmp_path/slow` containing `#!/bin/sh` and `sleep 5`, then expects `probe.parse([[str(slow), "--version"]])` to succeed and `probe.run` to execute it. This invokes `/bin/sh` despite the stated “no shell” constraint and despite `test_probe_refuses_what_is_not_declared_safe` expecting `["sh", "--version"]` to be refused. A descriptor that can name an arbitrary path can therefore bypass the shell ban by pointing to a shell script (or any executable), so the closed/declared-safe probe rule is not enforced by the behavior these tests assert.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_engines.py:test_probe_missing_binary_is_unavailable_and_timeouts_are_bounded

chunk_findings.detail: `render_json` now rejects `NaN`/`Infinity` literals on input, but the new output guard `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` is outside the `try` that converts JSON errors into `EngineError`. A syntactically valid JSON number that overflows to infinity, e.g. an existing file containing a sibling entry `"other": 1e999`, is loaded by `json.loads` as `float("inf")` because `parse_constant` is not invoked for numeric literals. Then `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` raises `ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant`, so a bad existing file crashes with an unhandled `ValueError` instead of returning text or raising `EngineError("the existing file is not JSON: ...")`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/mcp_shape.py:63

chunk_findings.detail: `_run_capped` does not stop processing the rest of a `select` result once the byte cap is crossed. With `limits.probe_output_bytes = 10`, if the child has 11 bytes ready on stdout and 65536 bytes ready on stderr, the first `os.read` appends 10 bytes and sets `total = 11`; the loop then reads stderr and evaluates `data[: limits.probe_output_bytes - total]`, i.e. `data[: -1]`, which appends 65535 bytes. The function returns roughly 65545 bytes and only then kills the child, so the declared output cap is bypassed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:_run_capped

chunk_findings.detail: The function computes `deadline` for the `select` loop but then calls `child.wait(timeout=limits.probe_timeout_s)` with a fresh full timeout after the pipes reach EOF. A probe that closes stdout/stderr at `probe_timeout_s - 0.05` and then sleeps for another `probe_timeout_s` causes the wait to run until nearly `2 * probe_timeout_s` before `stop_group` is called. The wait should use the remaining time from the original deadline, not a new full timeout.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:_run_capped

chunk_findings.detail: `_run_capped` uses `select.select` on pipe file descriptors. On Windows, `select.select` supports only sockets, so after `proc.spawn_stdio` succeeds the call raises `OSError` (e.g. WinError 10038) for any probe; because the exception occurs before the `stop_group` cleanup, the spawned child can also be left running. The parser explicitly treats backslash paths as Windows-style paths, so this is a defect in the intended cross-platform path handling.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:_run_capped

chunk_findings.detail: `is_shell` only removes a final `.exe` after lowercasing the last path component, so it does not handle Windows file-name forms whose trailing dot or space is stripped by the OS. Given the Windows launch template `["C:\\Windows\\System32\\cmd.exe.", "/c", "{prompt_file}"]` and values `{"prompt_file": "x"}`, `_lint` computes basename `cmd.exe.`, `removesuffix(".exe")` leaves it unchanged, and the value is not in `SHELLS`; the template is accepted. On Windows, the trailing dot is stripped during file-name resolution, so the accepted argv actually launches `cmd.exe`, violating the “no shell” invariant. A trailing space such as `cmd.exe ` has the same effect.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/render_argv.py:is_shell

chunk_findings.detail: `max_optional` is intended to bound the number of optional/alternation choices (`?` and `|`), but `_audit` adds `1` to `tally["narrow"]` for an entire `BRANCH` node rather than per alternative/pipe. With the shipped defaults, the pattern `a*(a|[a]|[aa])` repeated eight times followed by `a*b` (length 101, under `max_pattern_chars=200`) passes the audit: it has two wide repeats (`a*`), eight branch groups (`narrow=8`, not `>8`), and no repeat of a variable body. Calling `search(rx, "a" * 2048)` forces the regex engine to try the three alternatives in each of the eight groups across the two star splits before the trailing `b` fails, on the order of `3**8 * 2048**2` backtracks, so the new ReDoS limit is bypassed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/safety.py:_audit

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to guard the “length checked before `strip()`” fix, but its assertion cannot distinguish the two orderings. For the input `" " + "x" * 5000` with `Limits(max_line_chars=100)`, both the intended implementation (`len(line) > limit` before `line.strip()`) and the old implementation (`line.strip()` first, then the length check) return `None`; the only difference is that the old implementation allocates the large stripped copy. Because the test only asserts `is None`, it also passes with the old, unsafe ordering and therefore does not actually refute the earlier memory/allocation regression.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_engines.py:test_stream_map_checks_length_before_stripping

chunk_findings.detail: `big.write_text("#!/bin/sh\nhead -c 100000 /dev/zero | tr '\0' a\n")` uses the Python escape `\0`, so the generated script contains an actual NUL byte inside the `tr` argument instead of the shell characters `'\0'`. On common `/bin/sh` hosts (for example dash on Linux), a NUL byte in a quoted script string terminates the command/line, making the script malformed or giving `tr` an empty operand; the pipeline then produces no output or an error. In that case `probe.run` returns an unavailable/empty fact, so `assert f["truncated"] is True and len(f["output"]) == 100` fails. The same mistake at line 160 makes `test_third_review_findings` vacuous: if the malformed script produces no output, its assertion `len(f["output"]) <= 10` still passes without exercising the two-stream output cap.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_engines_review.py:199

chunk_findings.detail: The new probe regression tests are POSIX-only but are not skipped on non-POSIX hosts, even though the previous fix explicitly makes `_run_capped` return an unavailable fact on non-POSIX platforms. On Windows, `test_probe_programs_are_bare_names_and_output_is_read_capped` fails at `assert len(f["output"]) == 2000` because the probe is unavailable and the output is empty, and `test_fourth_review_findings` fails at `assert f["truncated"] is True and len(f["output"]) == 100` for the same reason. Additionally, `test_a_failed_spawn_leaks_no_descriptor` fails immediately on hosts without `/proc/self/fd` (e.g. Windows/macOS) when `fds()` calls `os.listdir("/proc/self/fd")`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_engines_review.py:test_probe_programs_are_bare_names_and_output_is_read_capped

chunk_findings.detail: `is_shell("/bin/ash")` returns `False` because `SHELLS` omits common shells such as `ash` (the default shell on Alpine). Thus `_lint` accepts `["/bin/ash", "-c", "echo hi"]`; the rendered argv then runs a shell despite the module’s “never a shell” guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: `render_argv.py:is_shell`

chunk_findings.detail: For `env={1: "SECRET"}`, the iteration yields `child=1`, and `not _ENV_NAME.fullmatch(child)` calls `re.Pattern.fullmatch` with an `int`, raising `TypeError` instead of the intended `EngineError`. The validation should check `not isinstance(child, str)` before calling `fullmatch`, as it already does for `source`.
chunk_findings.title: `render_argv.py:render`

chunk_findings.detail: In `_children`, for `_c.BRANCH` the parsed operand is `(None, alt1, alt2, ...)`, but the function returns `list(av[1])` instead of `list(av[1:])`. This makes `_audit` traverse only the first alternative of a `|` branch, so any later alternative is never checked for nested quantifiers or back-references. Concretely, `safe_regex(r"b|(a+)+!")` passes the audit because only the harmless first alternative `b` is inspected, then `re.compile` accepts the catastrophic second alternative. On the default limits, `search(compiled, "a"*2048)` makes the engine backtrack over all 2048 `a`s, defeating the ReDoS protection this module is intended to provide.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/safety.py:57 (_children)

chunk_findings.detail: `parse_rules` accepts `when.equals = None` (`Rule.equals` is typed `str | int | float | bool | None`), but `_matches` returns `v is not None and type(v) is type(rule.equals) and v == rule.equals`. Since `_dig` returns `None` both for a JSON `null` and for a missing path, the first conjunct is `False` for a line like `{"x": null}`, so `map_line` returns `None` and no event is emitted. The `exists` predicate has the same problem at line 78: a present JSON `null` is treated as absent. Thus a valid accepted rule using `null` is silently dead.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/stream_map.py:78,81

chunk_findings.detail: The test aims to ensure `stream_map.map_line` checks the line length before stripping, but the input `" " + "x" * 5000` with `Limits(max_line_chars=100)` has a stripped length of 5000, which still exceeds the limit. Therefore an implementation that strips first and then applies the length check would also return `None`, so the test passes regardless of the ordering it claims to enforce. A distinguishing input would be one with pre-strip length > 100 and post-strip length ≤ 100, such as `" " * 5 + "x" * 96`; the current test cannot detect a strip-before-length-check regression.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_engines.py:test_stream_map_checks_length_before_stripping

chunk_findings.detail: When the output cap is reached, the new code only stops reading (`if total >= limits.probe_output_bytes: break`) and then waits for the child to exit; it does not set `timed_out` or call `proc.stop_group` at the cap. Given an allowed probe command that writes more than the pipe buffer (for example a bare-name tool on PATH that writes 1 MiB to stdout and then exits), the parent reads up to `probe_output_bytes`, stops reading, the child blocks on the full pipe and cannot exit, and `child.wait(max(deadline - time.monotonic(), 0.01))` waits until the timeout deadline before killing the child and returning `None`. `run` then emits `status="unavailable", reason="timeout"` with no `truncated` field. This contradicts the docstring/run comment that output past the cap is stopped/killed and makes a huge writer consume the full probe timeout instead of producing a truncated result; the new `cut` flag is never true for this blocked-writer case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:_run_capped

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor fixes the `equals = null` half of the previous finding, but the `exists` predicate still cannot match a present JSON `null`. `_check_when` now rejects `equals: null` with the message “use exists”, yet `_dig` (unchanged by this diff) returns `None` for both a missing path and a JSON `null`, and the `exists` check uses `is not None`. Given a valid `emit` and a rule like `{"when": {"path": "x", "exists": true}, "emit": <valid event>, "fields": {}}`, the line `{"x": null}` produces no event. Thus `null` is unmatchable, and the new parse-time advice to “use exists” is wrong.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/stream_map.py:_matches

chunk_findings.detail: On POSIX systems without procfs (notably macOS, and containers where `/proc` is not mounted), the `skipif(os.name != "posix")` guard lets `test_a_failed_spawn_leaks_no_descriptor` run, then `fds()` executes `os.listdir("/proc/self/fd")` and raises `FileNotFoundError` before any probe descriptor-leak check is exercised. The test should be skipped unless `/proc/self/fd` is available (or use a portable fd-counting method); as written, the environment simply errors out.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_engines_review.py:178

chunk_findings.detail: `container_path` validates a shape only against `KeyError`, so an unhashable hostile shape crashes instead of producing an `EngineError`. For example, `mcp_shape.render_json([], "server", {})` reaches `CONTAINERS[shape]` and raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` before the `except KeyError` can convert the bad shape to the engine’s expected error type. The same applies to `entry`; a closed-set shape validator should reject non-string/unhashable values as `EngineError`, not leak a raw `TypeError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/mcp_shape.py:37

chunk_findings.detail: `SAFE_ARGS` includes the bare token `version`, which is not a switch. `parse` only checks that the argument is in this closed set, so `parse([["cat", "version"]])` is accepted and `run` executes `cat version`. If the probe’s current working directory contains a file named `version` (or, with an interpreter such as `python`/`node`/`ruby`, a script named `version`), this reads/prints that file or executes it instead of invoking a read-only version switch. That violates the stated “read-only switches” / “no shell” constraint: a descriptor can leak `./version` or run `./version` without naming a path or a shell.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:24

chunk_findings.detail: The read loop calls `select.select` after `proc.spawn_stdio` has started the child, but the cleanup that kills the child is only reached after the loop finishes normally. On common POSIX hosts, `select.select` raises `ValueError` when a descriptor is `>= FD_SETSIZE` (typically 1024); a ddflow process with many open descriptors can therefore get pipe fds above that limit. Given a long-running allowed program (e.g. an installed agent that hangs on `--version`) and >1024 open fds, line 100 raises after the child is spawned, the `finally` at line 109 only closes parent fds and does not call `proc.stop_group`, and `run` catches only `OSError`, so the probe raises `ValueError` instead of returning an unavailable fact and the child can be left running.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/probe.py:_run_capped

chunk_findings.detail: `is_shell` extracts the program basename by splitting only on `/` and `\`, so a Windows drive-relative path such as `C:cmd.exe` is treated as one whole component. After lowercasing and `removesuffix(".exe")` it becomes `c:cmd`, which is not in `SHELLS`; therefore `_lint` accepts `["C:cmd.exe", "/c", "{prompt_file}"]` and `render` returns an argv whose executable is a drive-relative path to `cmd.exe`. On a Windows host where the current directory on drive `C:` contains `cmd.exe` (for example `C:\Windows\System32`), this launches a shell, violating the “executable is never a shell” rule.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/render_argv.py:is_shell

chunk_findings.detail: `_audit` only enforces `max_repeat` when `hi != _c.MAXREPEAT`, so any repeat whose upper count is the unbounded sentinel bypasses the bound entirely, including the explicit lower bound in `{m,}`. With the shipped defaults, `safe_regex("a{1000,}")` is accepted even though `max_repeat=256`, because `hi` is `MAXREPEAT` and the code never checks `lo` against `limits.max_repeat`. That violates the stated limit on explicit repeat bounds and lets a descriptor force the regex engine to try to satisfy a large lower bound (e.g. `a{1000,}b`, or much larger counts) despite the audit claiming to cap such patterns.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/safety.py:_audit

chunk_findings.detail: `check_path` materializes the split result before applying the path-part bound: `parts = path.split(".")` is executed before `len(parts) > limits.max_path_parts` can reject the input. Given a hostile bad path such as `check_path("." * 1_000_000, "path")` with default `max_path_parts=16`, the function first builds a list of over one million parts (and for paths with large segments it also copies those segments) before raising `EngineError`. A bad path can therefore cause unnecessary memory amplification instead of being rejected cheaply by length/dot count.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/safety.py:check_path

chunk_findings.detail: The unknown-key error path can crash with `TypeError` instead of raising `EngineError` when the extra keys are not mutually orderable. For example, `expect_keys({1: None, "a": None}, {"b"}, "where")` computes `extra = {1, "a"}` and then calls `sorted(extra)`, which raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'`. This turns a validation failure into an unexpected crash whenever descriptor tables are allowed to contain non-string keys (e.g. from non-JSON loaders).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/safety.py:expect_keys

chunk_findings.detail: `map_line` parses each line with the default `json.loads`, which accepts Python’s non-standard `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity` constants (and can also turn overflowing numeric literals such as `1e999` into `inf`). For example, with `rules = parse_rules([{"when": {"path": "x", "exists": True}, "emit": "error", "fields": {}}])`, the call `map_line('{"x": NaN}', rules)` returns an `Event`, even though the line is not RFC 8259 JSON and should be skipped; with a field that extracts `x`, the returned `Event.fields` contains `nan`, which a downstream `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` (the mode used elsewhere in this change) will reject. The parser should reject non-finite constants/floats or use a constant guard like the mcp_shape engine.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/stream_map.py:98

chunk_findings.detail: `resolve_path` validates `session` with `_SEGMENT.fullmatch(session or "")`, which only behaves safely when `session` is a string or a falsy object that coerces to `""`. A truthy non-string session is passed directly to `re.Pattern.fullmatch` and raises `TypeError` instead of the intended `EngineError`. For example, with `spec = transcript_map.parse({"path": "{session}", "format": "jsonl", "fields": {"role": "role"}})`, calling `resolve_path(spec, session=1)` raises `TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'int'`; similarly `session=[".."]` raises `TypeError` from `fullmatch`. The same validation-layer crash occurs for truthy non-string `home`/`dir` at line 69, where `vals[k].startswith("/")` raises `AttributeError` for e.g. `home=1`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/engines/transcript_map.py:65

chunk_findings.detail: The “two-stream 10-byte cap” regression test does not actually force the stderr stream to exceed the cap: the script writes only `err\n` (4 bytes) to stderr and then the test asserts only `len(f["output"]) <= 10`. A wrong `_run_capped` that caps stdout only and does not enforce the cap on combined stdout+stderr (for example, it reads/caps stdout to 10 bytes and either ignores stderr or returns only stdout) passes this test, because stdout alone can be 10 bytes and the small stderr output cannot make the assertion fail. Thus the test cannot distinguish the intended combined-stream cap from a stdout-only cap; a hostile probe that writes more than 10 bytes to stderr would still violate the declared cap, but this test would not detect it. The script should produce more than the cap on stderr as well, and the test should assert that the combined output was actually produced and truncated (e.g. `f["truncated"] is True` and `len(f["output"]) == 10`).
